newsitem.title: ABU DHABI: China seeks missile sales to Iran, Gulf Arabs.
newsitem.headline: China seeks missile sales to Iran, Gulf Arabs.

text.p: China, which has angered Washington with its Iranian military ties, hopes to sell more missiles to Tehran and is seeking sales to Gulf Arab states, a Chinese industry official said on Wednesday.
But she said China was only interested in selling defensive weapons to Iran and its oil-rich Gulf Arab neighbours.
"We want to sell more missiles to Iran," said Chai Zhongzhong, assistant to the president of missile builder China National Precision Machinery Import and Export Corporation.
"Right now we are not in talks with Iran but we are hoping to sell them anti-aircraft and sea defence missiles," she told Reuters.

The United States has voiced concern over Chinese sales of missiles and related technology to Iran and Pakistan, possibly in violation of the Missile Technology Control Regime, a 31-nation pact designed to head off missile proliferation.

U.S. officials say Iran, which has restored its capability to fire anti-ship missiles at sea, has in the past two years tripled the number of missiles deployed on its Gulf coast and is fitting Chinese-built cruise missiles to 20 of its naval boats.
Chai said Chinese officials had made several visits to the United Arab Emirates over the past few years to hold talks and promote mainly sea defence missiles.
"They seemed interested. We held talks over the last several years, but they failed," she said on the sidelines of Abu Dhabi's international arms show IDEX 97.

Ties between the UAE and its powerful non-Arab neighbour across the Gulf have been strained by a sovereignty dispute over three Gulf islands located near key shipping lanes. Abu Dhabi has accused Iran of deploying offensive weapons on the islands, a charge denied by Tehran.
Chai said China was also hoping to sell missiles to other Gulf Arab states despite fruitless talks with the UAE.
"We think there is a market for us in all of the Gulf states," she said. "We are not in talks with other countries in the area but we plan to make more visits in the Gulf in the future."
She and other Chinese industry officials are hoping to use the IDEX show, which has lured 750 companies from 53 countries, to promote their military hardware.
Chai said China's past missile sales to the Gulf Arab region were "not much", but would not elaborate.

Paul Beaver, an arms industry expert with Jane's Information Group, said China's history of military sales to Iran was likely to undermine complicate its sales pitch to Gulf Arab states concerned about Tehran's military might.
"China is a major supplier to Iran. It has given them fast patrol boats and is involved in missile upgrades. This is a major problem. This will taint that flavour of the Gulf Arab states," he said.
"It will also be difficult for a country like the UAE that is modernising rapidly to see a country like China as a reliable supplier."
Beaver estimated that China had sold Iran several hundred missiles in the past ten years.
